lesson.title: Cortes, Pizarro, and the Fall of Two Empires
lesson.summary: This section explains how small numbers of Spanish conquistadors, led by Hernan Cortes and Francisco Pizarro, brought down the powerful Aztec and Inca Empires within little more than a decade, through a combination of alliances with rival indigenous groups, superior weaponry, and devastating epidemic disease.
lesson.body:
In the decades following Columbus's voyages, Spain sent waves of soldiers, adventurers, and fortune seekers, known as conquistadors, to explore and conquer territory across the Caribbean and mainland Americas. Two campaigns stand out for their consequences: Hernan Cortes's conquest of the Aztec Empire and Francisco Pizarro's conquest of the Inca Empire, both accomplished by remarkably small Spanish forces against empires that, on paper, commanded far greater manpower and resources.

Cortes landed on the coast of Mexico in 1519 with several hundred men. Rather than relying on Spanish numbers alone, he quickly recognized and exploited deep resentment among peoples who had long resisted Aztec tribute demands, most importantly the Tlaxcalans, longtime rivals of the Aztec state, who became crucial allies supplying thousands of warriors. Cortes also relied heavily on Malintzin, an enslaved Nahua woman given to the Spanish who became his interpreter and advisor, without whom communication with Moctezuma's court would have been impossible. After initially entering Tenochtitlan and taking Moctezuma hostage, Cortes and his forces were driven from the city in June 1520 during a night of heavy losses the Spanish later called the Noche Triste, the sad night. The Spanish returned within a year, joined by tens of thousands of indigenous allies, and by then a smallpox epidemic, introduced by the newcomers and detailed in the next section, had already devastated the city, killing Moctezuma's successor Cuitlahuac and weakening Aztec resistance. After a lengthy siege, Tenochtitlan fell on August 13, 1521.

A little over a decade later, Francisco Pizarro applied a similar combination of factors against the Inca Empire, which stretched along the Andes Mountains of western South America. Pizarro arrived in Peru with only a small force, but he benefited enormously from timing: a devastating epidemic, likely smallpox spreading ahead of direct Spanish contact, had already killed the reigning Inca emperor Huayna Capac around 1527, triggering a bitter civil war between his sons Atahualpa and Huascar. In 1532, Pizarro captured Atahualpa, who had just won that civil war, at the city of Cajamarca. Although the Inca ruler offered an enormous ransom in gold and silver for his freedom, one of the largest ransoms in recorded history, Pizarro had him executed in 1533, and Spanish forces went on to seize the Inca capital of Cusco.

It is tempting to explain these conquests purely through Spanish technological superiority, steel weapons and armor, firearms, and horses, none of which existed in the Americas before contact. These advantages mattered, but they do not fully explain how a few hundred men repeatedly defeated empires of millions. The deeper explanation is a combination of factors: disease that killed rulers and soldiers alike before battles were fought, deep political divisions that Spanish leaders skillfully exploited, and alliances with indigenous nations who saw the Spanish, at least initially, as useful partners against their own rivals rather than a shared threat.

The conquests of Mexico and Peru established the pattern for Spanish colonization across much of the Americas: the imposition of the encomienda system, which forced indigenous communities to provide labor and tribute to Spanish colonists, the extraction of enormous quantities of silver and gold, and the beginning of centuries of Spanish colonial rule that fundamentally reshaped the political and demographic map of the Western Hemisphere.
